name: The Worst Job Interview
blurb: The questions get stranger and stranger, until it is clear who is really being tested
title: The Worst Job Interview: Funny Skit Script for 3 People
description: A 5-minute comedy skit script for 3: a job interview with ever more absurd questions and a twist on who is interviewing whom. Free to perform.
h1: The Worst Job Interview: a 5-Minute Comedy Skit Script for 3 People
logline: Alex arrives for a simple office job and faces an interviewer who asks about kitchen appliances, umbrellas and animal noises. Meanwhile, a cleaner mopping the floor keeps giving better answers than anyone. When Alex finally walks out, the interview turns around completely.
setting: A small office. Props: a desk, two chairs, a clipboard, a folder, a mop and a bucket (a broom works too).

roles.name: Dana
roles.note: Adult, any gender. The interviewer. Takes every ridiculous question completely seriously.

roles.name: Alex
roles.note: Adult, any gender. The candidate. Polite, nervous, wants a normal job and a normal conversation.

roles.name: Pat
roles.note: Adult, any gender. The cleaner, humming, mopping, with perfect answers. Secretly the owner.

script.scene: SCENE 1 – A small office with one desk and two chairs

script.action: DANA sits behind the desk, reading from a clipboard with great importance. ALEX enters, neat and nervous, holding a folder.

script.say: Hello. I'm Alex. I'm here for the assistant job?
Sit. Do not touch the chair yet. Just look at it.

script.action: Alex looks at the chair. Dana writes something down.

script.say: Good. You may now touch the chair.
I brought my CV. I have three years of office experience, I can use most computer programs—
First question. If you were a kitchen appliance, which one would you be, and why are you lying?
I'm sorry?
Answer the first part.
A kettle? Reliable. Warm. Gets the job done.
Defensive. Now the second part.
I'm not lying!
That's exactly what a kettle would say.

script.action: PAT enters with a mop and bucket, humming, and begins mopping slowly around the desk.

script.say: Don't mind me.
Second question. How many umbrellas could fit in this room?
Open or closed?
Nobody has ever asked that.
Closed... maybe four hundred?
Three hundred and twelve. Open, nine. You'd need the door shut.

script.action: Dana and Alex both look at Pat. Pat keeps mopping.

script.say: Third question. Please describe your greatest weakness, using only animal noises.
Is this a real question?
Every question is a real question. This is a real office.

script.action: Alex takes a breath, then makes a small, sad sheep noise.

script.say: Perfectionist. Classic.
How did you get perfectionist from that?
It was the way the sheep went up at the end.
Exactly. Thank you.
Can I ask what the job actually involves?
Questions are my department. Fourth question. You are trapped on an island with only a stapler. What do you staple first?
I don't... the island?
Nobody staples the island.
I'd staple the instructions to the stapler. People always lose those.
Excellent answer.
The cleaner isn't even being interviewed!
Fifth question. Sing the sound your computer makes when it turns on.
No.
Then hum it.
No. I'm sorry. I came here for a real job. I've answered about a kettle, umbrellas, a sheep and a stapler, and nobody has looked at my CV once.

script.action: Alex stands and picks up the folder.

script.say: I don't think this company is for me.

script.action: Pat stops mopping. Leans the mop against the wall. Takes the clipboard out of Dana's hands.

script.say: Sit down, both of you.
Pat, I'm in the middle of—
Sit down, Dana.

script.action: Dana sits. Alex sits. Pat sits behind the desk. Pat looks at the clipboard.

script.say: Dana, this morning I gave you a list of the silliest questions I could write. I told you it was the company's official list. I wanted to see one thing.
Whether I could ask them with confidence?
Whether you would ask them at all.
You're not the cleaner.
I own the company. I mop on Thursdays. It's relaxing, and people say things around a mop that they never say around a boss.
So this was my interview.
For manager. You followed a ridiculous list without asking one question. You asked a person to be a sheep.
A sad sheep.
And you. You asked "open or closed". You asked what the job was. And when it stopped making sense, you stood up. That's who I want in charge of interviews.
In charge? I applied to be an assistant.
Now you're the person who decides who gets hired. Starting now.

script.action: Pat hands Alex the clipboard and stands, picking up the mop again. Alex looks at the clipboard, then at Dana. Alex moves to Dana's old chair behind the desk. Dana takes the candidate's chair.

script.say: I'd still like to apply for something. Anything.
Of course. Let's begin.

script.action: Alex looks at the clipboard. Thinks. A small smile.

script.say: First question. If you were a kitchen appliance, which one would you be?

script.action: Dana opens and closes their mouth. Pat, mopping, laughs out loud. Blackout.

ul: Desk centre stage, angled slightly to the audience. Dana behind it, the candidate's chair in front and to the side, so both faces are visible.
Pat mops in slow circles around the desk and comes closer with every question. By the stapler question Pat should be right beside Alex.
The turn starts when Pat leans the mop on the wall. Make that action slow and clear; the whole room should change in that moment.
The chair swap is the visual payoff: Alex walks behind the desk, Dana moves to the candidate's chair. Do it in silence.
Costumes: Dana in a jacket, Alex in a smart shirt, Pat in an apron or work gloves. A clipboard is the symbol of power, so pass it from hand to hand clearly.
Dana never thinks the questions are strange. Ask them like a serious, tired professional. The comedy is in the confidence.
Alex is the audience. Play each reaction honestly: confusion, then trying hard, then patience running out. Do not play it silly.
Pat's answers are thrown away while mopping, never looking up. If Pat waits for a laugh, the secret is spoiled.
The sheep noise needs a pause before it. Let Alex decide, breathe, then make one small, sad sound.
After Pat says I own the company, give Dana a long, quiet beat. The realisation is funnier than any line.
Last line: Alex should not sound mean. A small, kind smile, as if testing whether Dana will ask about the question.
Set it at a school: a student council interview, a nervous student, and the school caretaker who turns out to be the head teacher.
With four or five people, add a second candidate waiting outside who is brought in at the end and gets the first question from Alex.
Different ending: Alex refuses the boss job and asks Pat for the mopping job instead, because Pat clearly has the best day in the building.

prompts.keyframe: A serious interviewer at a small office desk reading from a clipboard, a nervous candidate in a smart shirt on a chair, a cleaner with a mop in the background, flat office lighting, wide shot, cinematic still, 16:9
shots: Medium two-shot, static, a candidate makes a small embarrassed sound while the interviewer writes notes very seriously, comedic awkward mood
Wide shot, slow push in as a cleaner leans a mop against the wall and takes the clipboard from the interviewer, tension shift, quiet power
Over-the-shoulder shot, the former candidate now sits behind the desk with the clipboard and smiles while the former interviewer sits nervously opposite

faq.q: Is The Worst Job Interview free to use on YouTube or in a drama competition?
faq.a: Yes. It is licensed CC BY 4.0. Perform it, film it, post it on monetised channels or enter it in competitions. Just credit "Script: cv.cm".

faq.q: Can we write our own absurd interview questions?
faq.a: Please do. Keep the order of rising strangeness: a strange but answerable question first, then one that needs a performance like the animal noises, then one that makes no sense at all. Pat should always have a calm, perfect answer.

faq.q: How long does it take to rehearse?
faq.a: It runs about five minutes. Two or three rehearsals are usually enough: one to learn the lines, one for timing the mop and the chair swap, and one full run with an audience of friends.
